c.tagline: Capital of the New South, where hip-hop, soul food, Civil Rights history, and a leafy urban forest converge.

taxi.fareNote: Metered fares apply in the city, but licensed taxis charge a fixed flat rate (around $40 for one passenger) between the airport and Downtown/Midtown. Ride-hailing apps are widely used and usually cheaper.

emergency.note: 911 is the single number for police, fire, and medical emergencies across the US.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: Caution in parts of downtown at night and some south/west neighborhoods

hood_desc: Atlanta's compact core packed with the city's headline attractions - Centennial Olympic Park, the Georgia Aquarium, World of Coca-Cola, the College Football Hall of Fame, and the Center for Civil and Human Rights; best for first-timers who want the big sights within walking distance.

The city's cultural and nightlife spine, home to the High Museum of Art, the Fox Theatre, sprawling Piedmont Park, and a dense strip of restaurants, rooftop bars, and clubs; suits travelers who want dining and going-out steps from their room.

Atlanta's affluent uptown district of luxury shopping (Lenox Square, Phipps Plaza), upscale dining, and high-energy nightlife amid gleaming towers and leafy estates; ideal for shoppers and those wanting a polished, upscale base.

A hip, fast-gentrifying neighborhood strung along the Eastside BeltLine trail, anchored by Ponce City Market's food hall and shops, Krog Street Tunnel street art, and the MLK Jr. birth home and historic site; draws younger travelers and creatives.

A charming, walkable residential village of bungalow-lined streets, independent boutiques, cozy cafes, and neighborhood bars centered on the Virginia and Highland avenue intersection; suits those wanting a relaxed, local feel away from downtown.
lodging: Omni Atlanta Hotel at Centennial Park
Days Inn by Wyndham Atlanta Downtown
AC Hotel Atlanta Buckhead at Phipps Plaza

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink throughout the city.

transit.hours: MARTA rail runs roughly 5am to 1am on weekdays (later on weekends); buses vary by route. The Atlanta Streetcar loops Downtown from morning until around 11pm.
transit.note: MARTA rail is the backbone for reaching the airport, Downtown, Midtown, and Buckhead, but the network is limited and much of metro Atlanta remains car-dependent.
transit.pay: Pay with a reloadable Breeze card ($2) or a single-use Breeze ticket ($1) loaded with fare value; a one-way ride is $2.50 and includes up to four transfers between rail and bus. Contactless tap-to-pay is rolling out under MARTA's new fare system.

transit.m: MARTA Red/Gold Line rail to Five Points/Downtown (~18 min)
Taxi flat rate to Downtown (~20-30 min)

tip.r: 18-20% at sit-down restaurants; $1-2 per drink at bars; 15-20% for taxis and rideshares.

food.name: Southern fried chicken
food.desc: Crisp, heavily seasoned bird fried to order and served with mac and cheese, collards and cornbread. Atlanta's benchmark Sunday-dinner plate.

places.name: Busy Bee Cafe
places.note: James Beard America's Classic; the same fried chicken recipe since 1947.

places.name: Paschal's
places.note: Civil rights-era institution; secret fried chicken recipe dating to the late 1940s.

places.name: Mary Mac's Tea Room
places.note: Open since 1945; tea-room fried chicken with a long list of Southern sides.

food.name: Lemon pepper wings
food.desc: Atlanta's own wing: fried whole wings dusted in lemon pepper, or ordered lemon pepper wet with buttery sauce. A citywide obsession.

places.name: J.R. Crickets
places.note: Credited with spreading lemon pepper wet; nearly 20 sauces and a devoted local crowd.

places.name: American Deli
places.note: Local chain widely called the original home of the lemon pepper wet wing.

places.name: Magic City Kitchen
places.note: Woman-owned kitchen whose wings are regularly ranked among the city's best.

food.name: Soul food meat-and-three
food.desc: Pick a meat - smothered turkey wing, oxtails, fried pork chop - plus three sides such as candied yams, collards and mac and cheese.

places.name: Busy Bee Cafe
places.note: The definitive ATL soul food plate; expect a line at lunch.

places.name: Old Lady Gang
places.note: Family-recipe Southern cooking, generous plates and a lively room.

places.name: Roc South Cuisine
places.note: Upscale reimagining of down-home Southern plates, praised for its fried chicken.

food.name: Fried green tomatoes
food.desc: Firm unripe tomatoes in cornmeal crust, fried and topped with remoulade or goat cheese. A Georgia classic on nearly every Southern menu.

places.name: South City Kitchen Midtown
places.note: Long-running Southern kitchen known for its goat-cheese-topped version.

places.name: The Colonnade
places.note: Old-school Southern dining room open since 1927; unfussy, generous cooking.

places.name: Mary Mac's Tea Room
places.note: Served alongside pot likker and cornbread in a classic tea-room setting.

food.name: Shrimp and grits
food.desc: Creamy stone-ground grits under sauteed shrimp with andouille, peppers and a peppery gravy. Coastal Georgia comfort food, city-style.

places.name: South City Kitchen Midtown
places.note: A signature dish here for decades; reliable and generously portioned.

places.name: Twisted Soul Cookhouse and Pours
places.note: Chef-driven soul food with a well-regarded shrimp and grits.

places.name: Poor Calvin's
places.note: Southern-Asian mash-up whose shrimp and grits is the most ordered plate.

food.name: Peach cobbler
food.desc: Georgia peaches baked under a buttery crust and served warm, usually with vanilla ice cream. The state dessert in restaurant form.

places.name: Mary Mac's Tea Room
places.note: Widely named the most popular place in Atlanta for peach cobbler.

places.name: Paschal's
places.note: The cobbler alone justifies a visit to this historic dining room.

places.name: Busy Bee Cafe
places.note: Classic homestyle cobbler closing out the city's most famous soul food plate.

food.name: Coca-Cola
food.desc: Invented in Atlanta in 1886 and still the hometown drink, taken ice cold, over crushed ice, or blended into a float.

places.name: World of Coca-Cola
places.note: Tasting room pours dozens of Coca-Cola products from around the world.

places.name: The Varsity
places.note: Drive-in since 1928; Coke and the famous Frosted Orange with chili dogs.

places.name: Mary Mac's Tea Room
places.note: Old-school room where Coke arrives cold in a glass at the table.

food.name: Sweet tea
food.desc: Black tea brewed strong and sweetened while hot, then poured over ice. Bottomless glasses are standard at Southern tables.

places.name: Mary Mac's Tea Room
places.note: Refills arrive without asking; the house tea is part of the ritual.

places.name: Busy Bee Cafe
places.note: Classic sweet tea to cut the richness of the soul food plate.

places.name: Paschal's
places.note: Served all day in a room that has poured it since the 1940s.

landmarks: Georgia Aquarium
One of the largest aquariums in the world, with a striking modern exterior and whale-shark-filled tanks inside.
World of Coca-Cola
An eye-catching branded museum near Centennial Park celebrating the drink invented in Atlanta.
Centennial Olympic Park
Built for the 1996 Olympics, its Fountain of Rings offers great shots of downtown skyscrapers reflected in the water.
Fox Theatre
A lavishly ornate 1929 Moorish/Egyptian-Revival theater whose glowing marquee is a Midtown Atlanta icon.
Martin Luther King Jr. National Historical Park
Includes Ebenezer Baptist Church and King's birth home, a moving and historically significant photo stop.
Piedmont Park
Atlanta's Central Park equivalent, where Lake Clara Meer frames the Midtown skyline beautifully.
Stone Mountain
A massive granite monadnock carved with a memorial relief, popular for its cable-car summit views.
Atlanta Botanical Garden
Lush gardens and the elevated Canopy Walk provide colorful, tranquil photo opportunities in Midtown.
High Museum of Art
Richard Meier's white porcelain-paneled building is a striking piece of modern architecture in itself.
Georgia State Capitol
A gold-domed 1889 Neoclassical capitol building that anchors downtown Atlanta's skyline.

train.note: Atlanta has exactly one passenger train: Amtrak's daily Crescent between New York, Washington, Charlotte, Birmingham and New Orleans. It calls at little Peachtree Station, 1688 Peachtree Road NW in Brookwood between Midtown and Buckhead, about three miles north of downtown and not on the MARTA rail network, so plan a taxi or rideshare. The station platform sits far below the building, reached by a long stairway or a lift, and the timings are awkward - southbound in the morning, northbound around 11pm. No international trains run anywhere near Georgia.

intl.to: Monterrey, San Luis Potosi, Guadalajara, Morelia & central Mexico

bus.note: Tornado Bus Company runs long-haul coaches from its Atlanta terminal deep into Mexico; the trip takes well over a day and you clear Mexican immigration at the border, so carry a passport and get an FMM tourist card. Domestic coaches use the Greyhound terminal on Forsyth Street beside Garnett MARTA station downtown, where Greyhound (https://www.greyhound.com/), FlixBus (https://www.flixbus.com/) and Megabus (https://us.megabus.com/) all pick up. Typical times are about two hours to Chattanooga, four to Birmingham, five to Nashville and ten to twelve to New Orleans. Tickets are cheapest bought online well ahead.

ferry.note: Atlanta is roughly 250 miles inland at around 1,000 feet of elevation and has no passenger ferry service of any kind; the only boats are pleasure craft and tour cruises on Lake Lanier and Lake Allatoona north of the city.

half.name: Lake Lanier
half.blurb: Large reservoir north of the city popular for boating, swimming, and lakeside hiking trails.

half.name: Helen
half.blurb: Alpine-themed mountain village in North Georgia with waterfalls, river tubing, and Bavarian-style architecture.

half.name: Dahlonega
half.blurb: Historic gold rush town and hub of Georgia's wine country, with vineyards and gold-panning attractions.

full.name: Blue Ridge
full.blurb: Small mountain town in North Georgia known for its scenic railway, downtown shops, and Appalachian views.

full.name: Providence Canyon
full.blurb: Erosion-carved gullies of rust-red and white sandstone nicknamed Georgia's Little Grand Canyon.
